title: Art, Forgery and Authenticity
description: Four extracts about art forgery: a discussion, a conservator at work, a debate about value and a philosopher on authenticity.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio discussion
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Helen, discussing forgery with an art historian, Dr Marsh.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Dr Marsh, you've written a book about some of the most successful art forgers in history. Let's begin with the obvious question. Why does forgery fascinate us so much?

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: I think it's because a good forgery undermines our confidence in our own eyes. We like to believe that we respond to beauty directly, but if a painting can move us for years and then be exposed as a fake, what exactly were we responding to? The forger embarrasses the expert, and there is a certain pleasure in that.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: You've said that forgers rarely copy existing paintings.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: That's right. The cleverest ones invent something new in the style of a famous artist, usually a work that fills a gap in the record, a missing early period or a lost subject. Experts want it to exist, you see. A forgery that confirms what scholars already hope is almost irresistible.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: So the gullibility is partly ours.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Very much so. One of the most notorious cases involved a painter who fooled leading authorities with works that, to modern eyes, look quite crude. The faces are strangely long, and the style is unmistakably of the nineteen thirties. But in their day the experts were so keen to discover a lost masterpiece that they saw only what they wanted to see.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: And did he profit enormously?

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: He did, but I would add that he claimed his motive was resentment rather than greed. He felt that the critics had dismissed his own paintings, and he wanted to prove them fools. He succeeded, though the consequences for him were ultimately severe.

parts.title: Part 2 · A conservator describes her work
parts.intro: You will hear a conservator, Ms Okoro, describing how suspected forgeries are examined.

script.speaker: Ms Okoro
script.text: When a painting arrives in my laboratory with a question mark over it, the first thing I do is look at it for a long time before touching anything. Experienced eyes pick up oddities in the handling of the brush, a hesitancy, a stiffness, that suggest someone copying instead of creating. But I never rely on instinct alone. A confident connoisseur can be spectacularly wrong.

script.speaker: Ms Okoro
script.text: So we turn to science. Pigments are the most valuable evidence, because every colour has a history. Certain blues, whites and greens were not manufactured until particular years. If we find a pigment in a painting dated to the seventeenth century that was only invented in the nineteenth, the case is more or less closed.

script.speaker: Ms Okoro
script.text: Clever forgers know this, of course, and some grind their own pigments from old materials or paint over genuine antique canvases, scraping away the original picture. That is why we examine the layers beneath the surface using X-rays and infrared light. Sometimes we discover a completely different painting hidden underneath, which can be quite moving.

script.speaker: Ms Okoro
script.text: Then there is the matter of time. Genuine old oil paint cracks in a particular pattern as it dries and ages. Forgers have been known to bake their canvases in ovens, or roll them around a cylinder, to imitate this. But artificial cracks tend to be too regular, and under magnification they give themselves away.

script.speaker: Ms Okoro
script.text: What I find humbling is that the very techniques we use today will eventually seem primitive. A forgery that passes our tests now may be unmasked in fifty years by methods not yet invented. Authenticity, in that sense, is never permanently certain. It is a provisional verdict, which we hold until something better comes along.

parts.title: Part 3 · A debate about value
parts.intro: You will hear a dealer, Mr Alvarez, and an art critic, Linh, arguing about whether a fake loses its value.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Let me put the puzzle simply. Imagine a painting that has hung in a gallery for fifty years and delighted thousands of visitors. Then it is revealed as a fake. Nothing about the object has changed, but suddenly it is worth almost nothing. Is that not absurd?

script.speaker: Mr Alvarez
script.text: It's not absurd, it's perfectly rational. What people pay for is not paint on canvas. They are paying for a connection to a particular person at a particular moment. A forgery cannot supply that, however skilful it may be.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: But if the pleasure is real, surely the experience has value, whoever made the picture. We don't refuse to enjoy a symphony because it's performed by an orchestra we've never heard of.

script.speaker: Mr Alvarez
script.text: That's a false comparison. A performance is meant to be repeated. A painting is a trace of one individual's hand, and there is only one of it. If I told you that a stranger had faked your grandmother's letters, would you say it makes no difference because the words are the same?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That's rather unfair. Letters are personal, whereas pictures are public. And a good copy can educate people who will never see the original.

script.speaker: Mr Alvarez
script.text: A copy that's honestly labelled can do that, I agree. What offends me is the deceit. Selling a fake as genuine is a lie, and it harms scholarship, because it pollutes the record that future historians depend on.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I'll grant you that. If the fraud is the wrong, then the thing to condemn is the lie, not the beauty. But I still think we should ask why we are so ready to stop liking something the moment its label changes.

script.speaker: Mr Alvarez
script.text: Perhaps because we never truly liked it in isolation. We liked what we thought it was. And I'd say that tells us something rather interesting about ourselves.

parts.title: Part 4 · A closing reflection
parts.intro: You will hear a philosopher, Dr Tran, reflecting on authenticity at the end of the programme.

script.speaker: Dr Tran
script.text: Let me end with a thought experiment. Suppose someone produces a perfect replica of a famous painting, atom for atom identical to the original. Is there anything left that the original has and the copy lacks? Many people feel that there is, though they struggle to say what. I think it comes down to history. The original is the thing that came from the artist's hand, in a particular time and with particular intentions.

script.speaker: Dr Tran
script.text: That suggests that authenticity is not a property you can see. It is a relation between an object and its origins. And that is why the discovery of a forgery changes our experience, even though nothing visible has changed. We now know how the object came to be, and our response alters accordingly.

script.speaker: Dr Tran
script.text: Some people find this troubling. They say that a response to beauty ought to depend only on what is in front of us. I am not convinced. When we admire a work of art, we are admiring an achievement, something that a person did against difficulty. A forgery, however skilful, achieves something different, a successful imitation. The two achievements deserve different kinds of respect.

script.speaker: Dr Tran
script.text: Having said that, I would resist the idea that forgeries are therefore worthless. The best of them are fascinating documents of their own time, telling us what experts wanted to believe. Several have been displayed in museums, labelled honestly, and they draw crowds.

script.speaker: Dr Tran
script.text: So perhaps the lesson is modest. The label matters, but it need not be the end of the story. A forged painting may cease to be a masterpiece and become something else, a mirror that shows us our own desires. That is not nothing, and I would argue that it is exactly what a thoughtful visitor ought to look at.

questions.text: According to Dr Marsh, why does forgery fascinate us?
options: It makes valuable art cheaper for ordinary buyers
It shows that real beauty is extremely rare
It shakes our trust in our own judgement
It is surprisingly easy to do well with practice
questions.explanation: He says a good forgery undermines our confidence in our own eyes.

evidence.quote: a good forgery undermines our confidence in our own eyes

questions.text: What kind of work do the cleverest forgers produce?
options: Paintings in their own personal style
New works that fill a gap in the record
Drawings of landscapes by lesser-known artists
Exact copies of famous paintings in museums
questions.explanation: They invent something new in the style of a famous artist that fills a gap.

evidence.quote: usually a work that fills a gap in the record

questions.text: What does Dr Marsh suggest about the experts in the notorious case?
options: They were dishonest about the paintings they praised
They saw what they wanted to see
They were never fooled by his crude style
They were too young to know his period
questions.explanation: He says they were so keen to discover a masterpiece that they saw only what they wanted to see.

evidence.quote: they saw only what they wanted to see

questions.text: What is Dr Marsh's overall view of forgery?
options: Forgers are always clumsy and easy to spot
Experts' hopes make them easy to deceive
Forgery is purely a modern problem for museums
Museums are careless about checking their works

A desperate need for money to survive

To see layers beneath the surface

questions.text: How can artificial cracks be recognised?
options: They appear only on the frames, not the canvas
They tend to be too regular under magnification
They are too small to be seen with the eye
They are too deep compared with natural cracks

evidence.quote: artificial cracks tend to be too regular

questions.text: What does she find humbling?
options: Today's techniques will one day seem primitive
Experts often disagree about the same painting
Forgers are becoming much rarer these days
Her laboratory is small and poorly funded

questions.text: What puzzle does Linh describe?
options: A fake that was loved becomes worthless overnight
A fake that is cheaper than a good copy
A gallery that sold its collection after fifty years
A real painting wrongly condemned as a fake
